title: Bread on the deck (Acts 27:27–44)
hookLine: Paul urges everyone to eat, gives thanks, and all 276 reach land
tomorrow: soaked and freezing on a strange beach. who lights the fire?

cards: When everything at home is falling apart, somebody usually forgets to eat. Acts 27 reaches that moment.
It's the fourteenth night, the rocks are close, and "they cast four anchors out of the stern, and wished for the day." Before dawn, Paul talks about breakfast.

You've gone fourteen days without a meal, he tells them: "Wherefore I pray you to take some meat: for this is for your health". Meat, in the King James, means food. Then he does something readers still take two ways.

teach.b: Here's the line: "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat."

teach.h: ONE VIEW: AN ECHO OF THE SUPPER.
teach.b: One reading hears the Last Supper. In Luke's Gospel, Jesus "took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it." Same steps: took, thanked, broke.

teach.h: ANOTHER: A PLAIN MEAL, ON PURPOSE.
teach.b: On this view, something holy happens on that deck: thanksgiving in the middle of a storm, and a meal that points back to Jesus' table. The other reading says: look who's on board.
Two hundred and seventy-six hungry sailors, soldiers and prisoners, nearly none of them believers that Acts mentions.
Paul isn't leading a service; he's a man giving thanks before food, out loud, and eating first so the others will. On this view the plainness is the point.

teach.h: ALL OF GOOD CHEER, AND FED.
teach.b: Both readings agree on what happens next: "Then were they all of good cheer, and they also took some meat." Yesterday's words moved from Paul's mouth into everybody's body.
Acts counts them: "two hundred threescore and sixteen souls." The ship strikes and the stern breaks. Some swim; the rest come in on boards and broken pieces.
"And so it came to pass, that they escaped all safe to land."

how: Some Christians say a short grace before meals; in hard times, giving thanks together before eating is one way families and churches keep going.

games.q: what does “bread on the deck” mean?
o: the Last Supper Jesus shared in an upper room
a meal Paul blessed before dawn on a sinking ship
bread the disciples shared on the Galilee shore

games.q: before dawn on the deck — tap the pairs.
p: what Paul did with the bread

s: Acts says Paul's bread on the ship was communion
Acts doesn't say. some readers hear the Last Supper; others read a plain meal.
after Paul ate, the others took heart and ate too
then were they all of good cheer, and they also took some meat.
meat in this King James verse means animal flesh
here it means food, any food: take some meat, for your health.

games.q: your friend says Acts 27:35 is obviously communion on a ship. give the best case for the other reading.
o: most on board weren't believers; a plain meal with thanks is the point.
Paul forgot the bread was holy because of the storm.
Acts never actually mentions bread on the ship.
games.why: the plain-meal reading looks at who's on board: sailors, soldiers, prisoners. both readings agree that thanks were given and everyone ate and took heart.

practice: Take a glass of water or something small to eat, and hold it a moment before the first sip. Give thanks for it, out loud or under your breath, and for one person in this hard stretch with you.
Then taste it slowly, and let the rest of the sit be quiet.

wordCard.voice: Bread on the deck. Bread taken, thanks given, and everyone on a breaking ship fed before dawn.

orig.note: Greek: he gave thanks. In Acts 27:35, as Paul takes the bread.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: all came safe to land, some swimming, some on broken pieces. Rest well.
